modules.title: DDL — CREATE, DROP, ALTER
modules.goal: Define and modify the structure of database tables themselves, rather than the data inside them.
keyConcepts: **CREATE TABLE** defines a new table's columns and their data types.
**ALTER TABLE** changes an existing table's structure — e.g. adding or dropping a column — without touching its data.
**DROP TABLE** permanently deletes a table and everything in it; there's no undo.
modules.proTip: DROP TABLE has no confirmation step in most databases — always double-check you're targeting the right table (and environment) before running it.

modules.title: DML — INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE
modules.goal: Add, modify, and remove the actual rows of data inside a table.
keyConcepts: **INSERT** adds new rows; you can specify exact columns or provide values for all of them in order.
**UPDATE** without a WHERE clause changes every row in the table — always pair it with a filter unless that's truly the intent.
**DELETE** removes rows permanently — like UPDATE, an unfiltered DELETE wipes the entire table.
modules.proTip: Before running an UPDATE or DELETE, run the same WHERE clause as a SELECT first to confirm exactly which rows you're about to affect.

modules.title: SELECT Basics
modules.goal: Retrieve specific columns (or all columns) from a table.
keyConcepts: **SELECT \*** returns every column — fine for exploring, but naming columns explicitly is safer in real applications.
**AS** renames a column or expression in the output without changing the underlying data.
modules.proTip: SELECT * is convenient while exploring a new table, but explicit column lists make queries more predictable when a table's structure changes later.

modules.title: WHERE — Filtering Rows
modules.goal: Narrow a result set down to only the rows that match a condition.
keyConcepts: WHERE runs **before** grouping — it filters individual rows, not aggregated groups (that's what HAVING is for).
**AND**/**OR** combine multiple conditions; **IN** and **BETWEEN** are shorthands for common comparison patterns.
modules.proTip: WHERE can't reference an aliased column defined in the same SELECT — that limitation is part of why HAVING exists for filtering after aggregation.

modules.title: Aggregation — GROUP BY
modules.goal: Collapse many rows into summary rows, one per unique value of a column.

example.code:
SELECT department, AVG(salary) AS avg_salary
FROM employees
GROUP BY department
HAVING AVG(salary) > 50000;

keyConcepts: Every non-aggregated column in SELECT must appear in GROUP BY.
**HAVING** filters groups after aggregation — it's to GROUP BY what WHERE is to individual rows.
modules.proTip: If you need to filter on a raw column value, use WHERE (runs first); if you need to filter on an aggregate result, use HAVING (runs after grouping).

modules.title: Sorting — ORDER BY
modules.goal: Control the order rows appear in a result set.
keyConcepts: **DESC** sorts highest-to-lowest; **ASC** (the default) sorts lowest-to-highest.
Multiple columns in ORDER BY break ties — later columns only matter when earlier ones are equal.
modules.proTip: Without ORDER BY, SQL makes no guarantee about row order at all — never rely on 'the order it happens to come back in'.

modules.title: Joins — INNER JOIN
modules.goal: Combine rows from two tables, keeping only rows that have a match in both.
keyConcepts: A row only appears in the result if it has a matching row on **both** sides of the join.
This is the default join type — writing just JOIN means INNER JOIN in most databases.
modules.proTip: If rows are unexpectedly missing from your results, check whether an INNER JOIN is silently dropping unmatched rows — a LEFT JOIN might be what you actually need.

modules.title: Joins — LEFT OUTER JOIN
modules.goal: Keep every row from the left table, filling in NULLs for any unmatched right-side columns.

example.code:
SELECT c.name, o.id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;

keyConcepts: Every left-table row appears at least once, whether or not it has a match on the right.
Filtering **WHERE right.col IS NULL** after a LEFT JOIN is the standard pattern for finding 'things with no match'.
modules.proTip: 'LEFT OUTER JOIN' and 'LEFT JOIN' are the exact same thing — the word OUTER is optional in virtually every SQL dialect.

modules.title: Joins — RIGHT OUTER JOIN
modules.goal: Keep every row from the right table, filling in NULLs for unmatched left-side columns — the mirror image of a LEFT JOIN.
keyConcepts: A RIGHT JOIN is identical to a LEFT JOIN with the table order swapped — many teams just swap tables and use LEFT JOIN for consistency.
Some databases support RIGHT JOIN less consistently than LEFT JOIN, which is part of why LEFT JOIN is more common in practice.
modules.proTip: You can always rewrite a RIGHT JOIN as a LEFT JOIN by swapping which table comes first — many teams do this purely for readability consistency.

modules.title: Joins — FULL OUTER JOIN
modules.goal: Keep every row from both tables, matched where possible and filled with NULLs where not.
keyConcepts: Combines the behavior of LEFT and RIGHT JOIN — nothing from either table is dropped.
Rows with no match on either side will have NULLs in the columns from the other table.
modules.proTip: SQLite doesn't support FULL OUTER JOIN natively — it's commonly emulated with a UNION of a LEFT JOIN and a RIGHT JOIN when needed.

modules.title: CASE Statements
modules.goal: Add conditional, if/else-style logic directly inside a query.

example.code:
SELECT name,
  CASE
    WHEN salary >= 80000 THEN 'Senior'
    WHEN salary >= 50000 THEN 'Mid'
    ELSE 'Junior'
  END AS level
FROM employees;

keyConcepts: CASE checks WHEN conditions **in order** and stops at the first match — order matters.
**ELSE** is optional; without it, non-matching rows simply get NULL instead of a fallback value.

blueprint.code:
CASE
  WHEN <condition> THEN <value>
  WHEN <condition> THEN <value>
  ELSE <default>
END AS <alias>

modules.proTip: CASE can be used anywhere an expression is valid — not just in SELECT, but also inside WHERE, ORDER BY, and even GROUP BY.

modules.title: Subqueries
modules.goal: Use the result of one query as an input to another — nesting a query inside a query.
keyConcepts: A subquery in the WHERE clause runs **once**, independent of the outer query's rows — that's what makes it 'non-correlated'.
Subqueries can appear in SELECT, FROM, or WHERE clauses, not just as filters.
modules.proTip: If a subquery only ever returns a fixed, independent result, it's usually clearer than a JOIN — but for row-by-row logic, a correlated subquery or JOIN is often the better tool.

modules.title: Correlated Subqueries
modules.goal: Run a subquery once per row of the outer query, referencing a column from that outer row.
keyConcepts: Unlike a regular subquery, a correlated subquery references a column from the **outer** query (here, `e.department`) — it can't run on its own.
Because it re-executes per outer row, correlated subqueries can be slower than an equivalent JOIN on large tables.
modules.proTip: A quick test for 'is this correlated?' — if it references a column from the outer table, it is; if it could run completely on its own, it isn't.

modules.title: CTEs (WITH clause)
modules.goal: Give a subquery a name and reuse it, making complex queries far easier to read than deeply nested subqueries.
keyConcepts: A CTE (Common Table Expression) is defined with **WITH** and behaves like a temporary, named result set for the rest of that query.
CTEs can be chained — you can define multiple, and later ones can reference earlier ones.
modules.proTip: CTEs don't persist beyond the query they're defined in — they're purely a readability tool, not a stored table.

modules.title: Window Functions
modules.goal: Compute values across a set of rows related to the current row, without collapsing them into groups the way GROUP BY does.
keyConcepts: **OVER (...)** is what makes a function a window function — it defines the 'window' of rows the calculation applies to.
**PARTITION BY** resets the calculation for each group, similar to GROUP BY — but unlike GROUP BY, individual rows aren't collapsed.
modules.proTip: RANK() leaves gaps after ties (1, 1, 3); DENSE_RANK() doesn't (1, 1, 2) — pick based on whether ties should 'use up' a rank position.
